summary: Microsoft Windows Developer blog post announcing general availability of Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), a policy-driven containment layer for AI agents on Windows, macOS and Linux. Developers and IT define which files, network destinations and UI an agent may use, and the OS enforces it outside the agent's control. Four backends are offered (process, session, WSL container, experimental MicroVM), plus Enforcement, Learning and Permissive modes. Entra identity for agents, Intune policy and Agent 365 controls are described as coming soon.
speakers_or_authors: Microsoft Windows Developer team (vendor blog, no named author)
relevance_reason: Directly about how OS-level agents that operate software on a PC are constrained and managed, which bears on the computer-use agents theme. It is a vendor announcement with no user evidence, and it is developer and IT focused rather than about how people work with agents.

claims.claim: Microsoft says MXC is now generally available and provides the containment layer for agents on Windows.
claims.quote: Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), now generally available, provides the containment layer.

claims.claim: Microsoft argues users face a false choice between unrestricted agent access and blocking agents, and that agents need a boundary enforced independently of themselves.
claims.quote: An agent cannot be its own security authority. It must run within a boundary defined by the developer or organization and enforced independently of the agent itself.

claims.claim: MXC policy sits outside the agent workload, so an agent or its generated code cannot grant itself extra access.
claims.quote: The policy remains outside the agent workload’s control, so the agent or generated code cannot grant itself additional access.

claims.claim: Only Windows offers a session container that runs the agent in a separate OS-isolated session with its own identity and separate desktop, clipboard, UI and input boundaries.
claims.quote: Only Windows supports a session container, which runs an agent on the user’s device in a separate, OS-isolated session with its own local agent identity

claims.claim: Intune policy for MXC process containers, Entra agent identity and Agent 365 controls for local agents are announced as coming soon, not yet shipped.
claims.quote: Intune policy will soon be available to manage MXC process containers used by MXC-integrated agents on Windows 11.

claims.claim: The MicroVM backend is labelled experimental, so the strongest isolation option is not yet a finished feature.
claims.quote: MicroVM | Windows 11 and Linux, experimental | Higher-risk workloads that benefit from a hardware-backed virtualized boundary.

claims.claim: On Windows, a Learning mode produces an activity report of blocked resource requests to help write least-privilege policies, because writing them is hard without knowing what an agent needs.
claims.quote: Writing a least privilege policy can be difficult when you do not yet know every resource an agent workload requires.

claims.claim: Microsoft says agents blocked by policy should explain the failure, request action or choose a safe alternative rather than failing silently.
claims.quote: the agent should explain that the task could not completed within the available permissions

commercial_interest: Vendor speaking about its own product (Microsoft promoting MXC, Windows 365, Intune, Entra and Agent 365). No independent testing or user evidence is presented.
older_event: No. The item announces GA on 2026-10-07; Entra, Intune and Agent 365 pieces are future ('soon').
